papers.title: Landslideagent with multimodal landslidebench: a domain-rule-augmented agent for autonomous landslide identification and analysis
papers.summary: Intelligent identification and analysis of landslides are critical for disaster prevention. However, current interpretation paradigms struggle to simultaneously extract visual features and geoscientific semantics, while general-purpose vision–language models (VLMs) suffer from perceptual limitations and domain hallucinations in complex geological scenarios. This paper proposes an instruction-driven agentic framework for landslide response that integrates a multimodal benchmark, a specialized VLM, and a rule-enhanced agent. First, a multimodal fine-grained landslide dataset LandslideBench with seven landslide subtype labels, high-resolution imagery, pixel-level masks, and high-quality textual descriptions is constructed through multi-VLM cross-validation and interactive annotation. Second, a landslide-oriented dual-head vision-language method, LandslideVLM, is proposed and fine-tuned on LandslideBench via low-rank adaptation, in which a discriminative classification head and a generative language head are integrated to jointly support fine-grained landslide classification and geoscientific semantic description. Finally, a domain-rule-enhanced LandslideAgent is developed by integrating structured report metadata constraints and cross-validation identification constraints. Experimental results demonstrate that LandslideBench can serve as an effective benchmark for landslide interpretation. The fine-tuned LandslideVLM achieves accuracy improvements of 12.79%, 55.71%, and 17.27% on landslide discrimination, fine-grained classification, and semantic description quality, respectively. Across 28 paired cases, rule-constrained LandslideAgent achieves an accuracy of 88.7% across six evidence-checkable fields, outperforming free-mode agent by 11.9%.

papers.title: Cloudbursts and Floods in Nepal: Ecological Pathways, Evidence Gaps, and Consequences for Aquatic Fauna and Freshwater Ecosystems
papers.source: Journal of Global Agriculture and Ecology
papers.summary: This review assesses how cloudburst-associated flash floods, monsoon floods, and sediment-laden cascading floods impact aquatic fauna and freshwater ecosystems in Nepal. A synthesis of original research was conducted to connect hydroclimatic and geomorphic data to field observations of benthic macroinvertebrates, macrophytes, fishes, crocodilians, and river dolphins. Periodic monsoon flooding does not automatically equate to ecological degradation. For example, Nepalese stream invertebrates are capable of exhibiting population-level flexibility, and flood pulses are known to maintain channel-floodplain connectivity. However, the potential for degradation increases when rainfall, landslide sediment, and bank failure are combined with anthropogenic flooding. Buried fauna and flora experience both habitat homogenisation and disconnection during recovery. The strongest Nepal-specific evidence is for macroinvertebrate seasonality and habitat controls; direct indicators of the effects of cloudbursts on aquatic ecosystems are largely lacking. Post-flood surveys conducted in Koshi Tappu document the displacement and alteration of habitats of fauna, but do not support either mortality or biodiversity loss on a national scale. Fish and river dolphin studies have shown the importance of habitat depth, discharge, water quality, habitat connectivity, and dry season refuges on the fauna of aquatic ecosystems. The objective of this study is to assess how cloudburst-associated flash floods, monsoon floods, and sediment-laden cascading floods affect aquatic fauna and the ecological integrity of freshwater ecosystems in Nepal. The State of Nepal should use hydrometeorology and sediment measurements to guide before-after-control-impact studies of the effects of hazard mitigation practices. The conservation goal should be to protect aquatic ecosystems from fragmentation caused by emergency flood protection systems.

papers.title: Record warmth in the Sea of Japan amplified the September 2024 Noto heavy rainfall associated with a mesoscale low-pressure disturbance
papers.summary: Abstract In September 2024, record-breaking rainfall caused severe flooding and landslides in the Noto region, Japan, where recovery from the devastating Noto Peninsula earthquake was still ongoing. During this event, the Sea of Japan experienced record warmth, with monthly-mean sea surface temperature anomaly of + 2.9 °C. To quantify the impact of this anomalous ocean warming on the heavy rainfall, we conducted numerical sensitivity experiments using a regional atmospheric model in which only the sea surface temperature conditions in the Sea of Japan were replaced with those from each year between 1991 and 2020. Simulated rainfall over the Noto region was nearly twice as large under the observed 2024 SST conditions, indicating that the exceptionally warm ocean substantially amplified the event. The warming did not alter the occurrence or track of a mesoscale low-pressure disturbance along the autumn rain front, but the intensity of the disturbance systematically increased with SST and was accompanied by stronger southwesterly winds and moisture transport into the frontal zone. Ocea​nic analyses further showed a marked strengthening of the Tsushima Warm Current in 2024. These results highlight the importance of atmospheric responses to anomalously warm ocean conditions in amplifying extreme rainfall under anomalously warm ocean conditions and underscore the need to consider such processes in future risk assessments around Japan.

papers.title: Geomorphic calibration of friction and entrainment parameters for a snowmelt-induced muddy debris flow in the Longiarù Valley, Dolomites
papers.summary: Abstract Snowmelt- and rainfall-triggered debris flows are important geomorphic hazards in alpine environments, yet frictional and entrainment parameters are rarely available for individual events. This study constrains these parameters for a snowmelt-induced muddy debris flow that occurred in the Seres Creek catchment, Longiarù Valley, Dolomites, on 17–18 June 2024. A pre-event DEM from 2010 and a post-event LiDAR-derived DEM from 2024 were used to derive a DEM of Difference (DoD) and characterize the spatial distribution of erosion and deposition associated with the event. The observed geomorphic response was then used to constrain the internal friction, basal friction, turbulent friction, and entrainment parameters through iterative r.avaflow simulations. The calibrated parameter combination comprised an internal friction angle of 17°, a basal friction angle of 9°, a turbulent friction parameter of 10 m/s², and an entrainment coefficient of kg⁻¹. The resulting simulation reproduced the major spatial characteristics of the observed event, including the transition from erosion and channel incision in the upper and intermediate reaches to deposition downstream. Comparisons of selected turbulent friction and entrainment values showed that turbulent friction strongly affected flow mobility, erosion, and runout, whereas entrainment substantially influenced flow momentum, erosion, and the downstream position of deposition. Comparison of simulated and DoD-derived geomorphic changes along the main flow path and at three representative cross-sections showed good spatial agreement in the major erosion–deposition patterns, with relatively minor localized differences in erosion and deposition magnitude. The results show that spatially distributed geomorphic change can provide constraints on frictional and entrainment parameters beyond runout extent alone, providing a spatially informed basis for event-scale debris-flow modelling.

papers.title: Queer Resistance and Gender Fluidity in Nepali Short Stories
papers.summary: This research chapter studies the struggles of sexual minorities in contemporary Nepali short stories: Usha Sherchan’s Unexpected Flood and Landslide , Archana Thapa’s Bimarda (“Effeminate”) taken from the anthologies Tesro Rang , and Kathaputala respectively, and Samrat Upadhyay’s The Royal Ghosts , the title story from the anthology The Royal Ghosts . In these literary narratives, the central characters recurrently deviate from the conventional gender roles and identities. They refuse to be confined to the socially imposed gender identities of heterosexual males or females. The deviation leads them to miserable condition as they are obligated to face various forms of discrimination. Based on this problem, this study explores the reasons behind their deviation from conventional gender roles and identity, the consequences they face while dismantling the heterosexual gender identity, and the ways in which they subvert stereotypical gender expectations. Based on Judith Butler’s theory of gender performativity and Eve Kosofsky Sedgwick’s critique of binary sexual categories, this chapter argues that gender is not an inherent trait, but a socially constructed identity. Individual’s gender is shaped through his/her performance and reinforced by cultural and societal norms. Butler and Sedgwick argue that individual’s gender identity is fluid, performative, and socially regulated. Through this theoretical lens, the current research concludes that the central characters in the selected texts resist and redefine traditional gender norms. They endure fear, humiliation, and abuse due to the intolerant attitude toward the queer identity within the Nepali socio-cultural context.

papers.title: LaRaTh-Br: An Event-Based Probabilistic Framework for Modeling Rainfall Conditions Associated with Landslides
papers.summary: Rainfall-based models are widely used to support territorial landslide early warning systems, in which the occurrence of one or more landslides is assessed over predefined warning areas rather than at individual, known slopes. Their development, however, is strongly influenced by methodological choices related to rainfall-event definition, rainfall–landslide association, predictor construction, and model calibration, especially when operational landslide inventories contain uncertainties in the timing and location of reported events. Here, we present LaRaTh-Br (Landslide Rainfall Thresholds—Brazil), a modular R-based computational framework designed to standardize event-based rainfall–landslide analysis. The framework integrates rainfall-event identification from continuous precipitation records, spatial and temporal association between rainfall events and landslide records, generation of multiple rainfall descriptors, and probabilistic modelling and validation. LaRaTh-Br adopts the rainfall event as the fundamental analytical unit and explicitly represents both events associated and not associated with reported landslides. The framework was demonstrated through a retrospective event-level modelling application using ten years of operational rainfall observations and landslide records from Blumenau, southern Brazil. The application showed that event duration and mean rainfall intensity contained most of the discriminatory information, while antecedent rainfall provided complementary information and short-duration peak intensity produced limited additional gain. More importantly, LaRaTh-Br enables alternative rainfall-event definitions, rainfall descriptors, and modelling configurations to be evaluated within a common and reproducible workflow, providing a flexible basis for the continued development and refinement of probabilistic rainfall–landslide models as operational rainfall and landslide datasets expand in Brazil and elsewhere.

papers.summary: This repository contains the survey data and R replication code for the study “From Intention to Adoption: Climate Change Adaptation among Farmers in Central Colombia.” The dataset comprises survey responses from 360 smallholder farmers across 12 villages (veredas) in three departments of Colombia’s central region (Caldas, Quindío, and Risaralda, also known as the coffee-growing region), stratified by hazard history (drought, landslide, or no reported events) using records from Colombia’s National Unit for Disaster Risk Management (UNGRD, 2005-2021). For each of seven climate change adaptation practices (water source protection, agroforestry, soil cover, retaining walls, income diversification, formal credit/insurance, and loans from non-financial sources), the data include Protection Motivation Theory constructs (perceived severity, perceived vulnerability, self-efficacy, response efficacy, perceived monetary and time costs, resistance to change), intention to adopt, and current adoption status, together with farm- and household-level control variables (age, gender, marital status, education, income, farm size, land ownership, number of workers, presence of water bodies o the farm, forest resources on the farm, and village-level hazard and altitude exposure). The accompanying R script (intention-adoption_script.R) reproduces all tables and appendices reported in the manuscript: a fractional-response model of adoption intention (Stage 1), a Bayesian multivariate probit model of joint adoption across five main practices, corrected for the endogeneity of intention via a control-function approach (Stage 2), and a full set of robustness checks, including an ordered-logit re-estimation, a wild cluster bootstrap, exclusion-restriction tests, and a village-block cluster bootstrap of the entire two-stage pipeline. A companion data dictionary (the Codebook and Location_Codes sheets in data.xlsx) documents the coding and exact survey wording of every variable.

papers.title: Improved Mask R-CNN inventory mapping and multivariable geo-environmental assessment of rainfall-induced shallow landslides in mountainous Beijing, China
papers.summary: Extreme rainfall can trigger numerous small, boundary-fragmented and spatially clustered shallow landslides. This study combined improved instance segmentation with reproducible spatial analysis to map and assess shallow landslides associated with the 2023 ‘23.7’ rainstorm in Zhaitang Town, mountainous Beijing. An improved Mask R-CNN integrated a convolutional block attention module, a path aggregation feature pyramid network and Soft-NMS. Under the random tile-level test design, the model achieved 89.51% precision, 88.31% recall, an F1 score of 88.91% and a mean intersection over union of 80.03%; these are in-scene estimates rather than evidence of geographic transferability. The resulting inventory contains 8298 landslides covering 3.05 km². Analysis of the harmonized geospatial layers showed that kernel density > 69.5 landslides/km² occupied 6.42% of the valid study area and contained 48.90% of mapped landslides. Frequency-ratio analysis identified enrichment in Wumishan Formation Members 1–3, 400–800 m elevation, 30–60° slopes, east-to-southwest aspects and concave terrain. A presence–background logistic model using 8212 landslide locations and 48,553 valid fixed-seed background samples showed no independent association for cumulative rainfall (odds ratio [OR] 1.00 per standard deviation, p = 0.999) or hourly intensity (OR 0.91, p = 0.407) after adjustment. Elevation, slope, plan curvature, aspect and lithology remained associated. Rainfall×slope and rainfall×susceptible-lithology interactions were non-significant. Residual Moran’s I was significant at 1 km but non-significant at 2–4 km aggregation, whereas five-fold spatial-block validation varied among regions (ROC AUC 0.699–0.870). The results separate event attribution from within-event spatial association and demonstrate a transparent workflow from rapid inventory mapping to spatially diagnosed environmental assessment.

papers.title: The impact of population growth on land-use: a system dynamics model for sustainable land-use planning in the Elgon Region of Uganda
papers.summary: Land-use and land-cover change poses major environmental challenge in regions where population growth increasingly drives encroachment into ecologically sensitive landscapes. This challenge arises from the dynamics of interacting feedbacks among; demographic change, declining household land size, ecosystem degradation, and delayed institutional responses. Previous studies in the context of Uganda, have investigated these factors, either independently or in pairs, but not holistically. This study developed a system dynamics model to examine the impact of population-driven land-use dynamics in the landslide prone Elgon region of Uganda. A System dynamics method was used to simulate long-term system behaviour under alternative policy intervention scenarios for sustainable land-use planning. Results indicate that the steady increase in the number of households and decline in land per household are the dominant drivers of encroachment into wetlands and forests. Population growth drives significant conversion of natural ecosystems, with forest cover declining from 317 km² in 2020 to 247 km² (22.08%) by 2050 under business-as-usual scenario, amidst rising demand for agricultural land, housing, fuelwood, and infrastructure. Wetland follows a similar trajectory, decreasing sharply from 47.7 km² to 28.3 km² (40.67%) over the same scenario. These trends are reinforced by weak institutional capacity, limited enforcement, low community participation, and inadequate coordination among conservation actors, which collectively undermine effective policy implementation. The findings also highlight the risks of business-as-usual land management and underscore the need for strengthened institutional enforcement, and coordinated conservation interventions. By explicitly capturing feedback-driven dynamics and long-term system responses, the model offers a policy-relevant decision-support tool for evaluating alternative interventions and guiding sustainable land-use planning in population

However, these systems are increasingly threatened by glacier retreat, land-use transformation, and climate variability, which jeopardize long-term water security. This study presents an integrative narrative review of 58 peer-reviewed scientific publications published between 2011 and 2025, focusing on hydrological modeling, cryospheric dynamics, hydrometeorological monitoring, climate change impacts, and ecohydrological processes in tropical Andean mountain systems. Following a systematic selection process, the reviewed evidence was organized into five thematic areas: advances in hydrological modeling under data-scarce conditions, validation of satellite precipitation products, glacio-hydrological and cryospheric dynamics, hydroclimatic scenario simulation, and ecohydrological approaches. papers.summary: Soil underground loss (SUL) is a distinctive erosion process in karst regions, where soil infiltrates into underground conduits through bedrock fissures, posing a severe threat to land resources. This paper reviews the frontier theories and practice of SUL, clarifying its mechanisms driven by soil properties, geomorphological settings, hydrological constraints, and human disturbances such as vegetation destruction and land cultivation. Conceptually, SUL has evolved from a slope-scale subsurface process to a catchment-scale surface–underground continuum, necessitating an integrated definition. Current estimates of SUL’s contribution to total soil erosion vary widely due to methodological and scale discrepancies. Among influencing factors, slope gradient and rainfall intensity consistently emerge as dominant drivers, while fissure degree and rock exposure rate show context-specific effects, highlighting the complexity of factor interactions. Future research should prioritize integrating field tracing with simulation experiments, establishing long-term observation networks, developing process-based models embedding epikarst conduit geometry, and translating findings into targeted mitigation measures. Advancing these directions will provide robust support for rocky desertification control and sustainable land management in karst regions globally.

papers.title: Quantitative analysis of urban underground drainage pipeline service status under rainstorm disaster
papers.summary: Abstract Underground drainage pipeline (UDP) system is critical infrastructure for urban flood control and drainage. During extreme rainstorms, rainfall infiltration can alter pore-water pressure and soil-pipe interaction in the surrounding soil. These changes may affect the structural safety of buried pipelines under traffic load. To investigate the structural responses of buried pipelines during extreme rainstorms and provide a basis for emergency assessment, this study integrates full-scale mechanical test, finite element simulation, historical rainstorm scenarios, and a one-dimensional convolutional neural network (1D-CNN) data agent model. Firstly, full-scale pipeline mechanical tests are conducted, and test results are used to calibrate material parameters in numerical simulations; on this basis, a pavement-pipeline coupled numerical model is established to evaluate UDP structural responses under normal service state. Secondly, based on time-series rainfall data from historical rainstorm disaster in Beijing, China, 20 numerical working conditions are established to investigate the effects of pipe voids, burial depth, subgrade soil permeability, and pipeline diameter on structural responses under the coupled action of rainstorm and vehicle load. Finally, a dataset containing 2370 samples is used to develop the 1D-CNN model; this model achieves an MSE of 0.0003 and an R² of 0.9955 on the test set. The proposed framework provides structural response prediction and identifies potentially vulnerable locations, offering a quantitative reference for emergency inspection prioritisation and structural safety assessment of urban pavement-pipeline systems during extreme rainstorms.

papers.title: Closing the research–practice gap in waterlogging modelling through holistic systems thinking and spatially explicit simulation
papers.summary: Soil waterlogging is a major constraint to global crop production yet remains poorly integrated into agricultural monitoring and decision-support frameworks because waterlogging events are episodic and spatially heterogeneous, while existing modelling approaches largely address individual components of the problem in isolation. We argue that, alongside continued improvement in the representation of key processes, a major and under-addressed bottleneck lies in integrating existing modelling capabilities into an operational decision-support pipeline. Here we propose a conceptual, systems-oriented framework, intended for further development and testing rather than as an implemented decision-support system, that links spatially explicit hazard assessment, crop response simulation and multi-objective evaluation to support adaptation planning. We outline a three-stage modelling pipeline that identifies where and when waterlogging is likely to occur, evaluates alternative engineering, agronomic and genetic interventions, and quantifies trade-offs among productivity, profitability and environmental outcomes. We specify the information exchanged between stages, illustrate the pipeline with a literature-based example, and outline how it could be evaluated and how uncertainty could be handled. Finally, we identify key priorities for advancing waterlogging modelling, including improved process representation of drainage, raised beds, irrigation–groundwater interactions and other adaptation strategies, stronger integration across modelling domains, and closer alignment between modelling outputs and stakeholder needs, beginning with joint framing of the decision problem. By providing a structured pathway for integrating current and future modelling advances into decision support, this framework aims to accelerate the translation of waterlogging research into practical adaptation.

papers.title: Optimising Permeable Infrastructure Networks in Sponge City Design for Urban Flood Resilience Using Coupled Hydrological, Clogging and Lifecycle Modelling
papers.summary: Abstract Urban pluvial flooding is intensifying as impervious surfaces expand and extreme rainfall events become more frequent. Sponge city design (SCD) relies on decentralised retention and infiltration, yet planners still lack tools that (i) link the progressive, sediment-driven loss of permeability to maintenance actions, (ii) allocate permeable infrastructure across heterogeneous catchments and (iii) weigh flood-damage savings against lifecycle maintenance costs. This study couples the Storm Water Management Model (SWMM) with a Green–Ampt infiltration scheme modified by an exponential sediment-clogging factor and a lifecycle cost–benefit module. Four scenarios were tested on a synthetic 4.5 km² high-density urban catchment under a 50-year, 24-hour design storm: a pipe-only baseline, 30% permeable interlocking concrete pavers (PICP), 50% permeable infrastructure with bioretention, and an optimised network with subsurface detention and controlled underdrains. The model was calibrated against observed flow data (NSE = 0.88, PBIAS = + 4.2%, RSR = 0.32). The optimised network reduced peak runoff by 43.7% (from 42.6 to 24.0 m³ s⁻¹), reduced total runoff volume by 49.1% and delayed the runoff peak by 68 min. Without maintenance, PICP conductivity fell by 72% within three years, whereas twice-yearly vacuum sweeping sustained about 88% of the initial conductivity. Capital expenditure exceeded that of a conventional upgrade (US$18.4 million versus US$15.5 million), but the discounted payback period was 7.2 years and the 30-year benefit–cost ratio was 2.41; the dominant sensitivities were the flood-damage benefit and the discount rate. The results provide design, maintenance and fiscal guidance for municipal planners moving from reactive to proactive, sponge-city-based drainage planning.

papers.title: Geophysically-informed modelling and interpretation of cosmic-ray neutron sensing response to soil moisture spatiotemporal dynamics
papers.summary: Abstract. Soil moisture and its dynamics have direct hydrological and ecological impacts, from the local field scale to the regional and global scales. Working on a gently-sloping vineyard with grassed interrows, this study combines soil moisture monitoring from cosmic-ray neutron sensing (CRNS) and soil sensors, geophysical characterizations, and CRNS numerical simulations. Multi-scale electrical resistivity tomography and frequency-domain electromagnetic mapping highlight a fingering transition from a clayey substrate to a fractured-karstic marl, both overlain by a more worked and homogeneous soil. Together with ancillary weather data, this spatial information and the associated infiltration dynamics explain how CRNS and nearby soil sensors respond differently to precipitation, depending on season, soil conditions, and rainfall characteristics. This highlights the critical interplay between spatiotemporal soil moisture dynamics and CRNS signal nonlinearity and nonuniqueness. CRNS numerical modelling further investigates this interplay, specifically in terms of lateral dominance of drier regions and amplified sensitivity to moisture changes at the soil surface, here induced by light rainfall events. A theoretical generalization of the dry-dominance is provided, based on Jensen's inequality and a third-order Taylor expansion of the CRNS response function. Together, field observations and numerical modelling inform a conceptual soil hydrology model that describes the observed soil moisture spatiotemporal dynamics. The results reinforce the value of more spatially informed, hydrology-based CRNS applications, a key step toward capitalizing on recent CRNS methodological advances and achieving a better integration with soil moisture networks and multi-methodological hydrological observatories.

papers.title: Beyond design performance: hydrological indicators and the effects of rainfall magnitude and facility age on urban green infrastructure
papers.summary: Protocol for a systematic review and multilevel meta-analysis of the hydrological performance of urban green infrastructure (bioretention/rain gardens, permeable pavement, and green roofs). The review (1) synthesises the indicators used to evaluate GI hydrological performance and defines a core indicator set, and (2) pools GI effects on runoff volume, peak flow, and surface infiltration capacity with three-level random-effects models, testing whether these effects decrease with rainfall magnitude and with facility age, and whether reported maintenance moderates the decline with age. Field monitoring and calibrated modelling studies are analysed separately. Web of Science, Scopus, and the Korean Citation Index (KCI) were searched on 11 November 2026; after de-duplication, 9,246 records remain for title/abstract screening, which had not started at registration. Screening uses active learning (ASReview) with the SAFE stopping procedure for Web of Science and Scopus records and manual screening for KCI records. The protocol, search log, export files, and de-duplication script are attached to this registration.

papers.title: Dynamics of inorganic nitrogen cycling, redox conditions, and microbial community composition in a floodplain soil induced by a heavy rainfall after summer drought
papers.summary: Climate change is increasing the frequency of droughts followed by heavy rainfall in temperate regions, with important consequences for water flow, nitrogen transport, redox dynamics, and microbial activity in floodplain soils. We investigated these coupled responses in a field experiment on a fine-textured arable Gleysol after prolonged summer drought. A simulated heavy rainfall event was applied using D 2 O-labeled water as a hydrological tracer, followed by recurrent moderate irrigation with non-labeled water. Soil cores to 50 cm depth were collected from irrigated and dry control plots over 14 d and analyzed for soil water content, δ 2 H signatures, nitrate and ammonium masses, bacterial community composition based on DNA and RNA, and extracellular enzyme activities. Within two hours after the simulated heavy rainfall, labeled water had reached at least 50 cm depth, indicating rapid preferential flow through drought-induced shrinkage cracks. In contrast, ammonium remained largely retained and increased only in the uppermost soil layer, consistent with a short-term rewetting-induced mineralization pulse. Subsequent moderate irrigation was retained mainly in the topsoil, likely because shrinkage cracks had closed after initial wetting. Redox potentials declined after irrigation, and were associated with later changes in nitrate pools, although transformation rates were not directly measured. Bacterial community composition remained stable at both DNA and RNA levels, whereas β -glucosidase and exochitinase activities increased after irrigation. Overall, heavy rainfall after drought created a short hydrological window for rapid nitrate displacement through preferential flow pathways, potentially bypassing nitrogen retention

papers.title: Quantifying key parameter sensitivities for water table depth in hydrological schemes of CoLM-PSUADE at a mountain forest site
papers.summary: Accurately representing groundwater dynamics in land surface models (LSMs) is crucial for understanding water-energy cycles and assessing water resources. The CoLM-PSUADE framework was then applied to evaluate groundwater-related parameters using WTD observations from the Gongga Mountain site. papers.summary: Abstract. Groundwater is the largest store of liquid fresh water, yet because it is hidden beneath the surface, it is primarily understood through models of porous-media flow. Richards' equation, a physically faithful description of variably saturated groundwater flow, remains costly for basin-scale groundwater modelling. Consequently, operational models use reduced physics, either by assuming linearity or by using approximate solutions. Here, we introduce a scalable, open-source, three-dimensional solver for variably saturated groundwater flow implemented in G-ADOPT, an automated finite-element platform built on Firedrake. The implementation combines a locally conservative discontinuous Galerkin discretisation, Newton iteration with an exact Jacobian, implicit time integration through the Irksome library, used here with Backward Euler, and vertically lumped multigrid preconditioners designed for the extreme aspect ratios of production scenarios. Our scaling experiments show that the effectiveness of the preconditioner is controlled primarily by the physical regime in which the model is integrated. A single-level method (e.g., block-Jacobi ILU(0)) suffices at the short time steps of an infiltration study, but at seasonal time steps, the admissible time step decreases significantly under horizontal refinement. In a near-saturated profile without specific storage, such single-level methods do not converge at any tested step size. The nature of these interactions depends on individual tree species’ functional traits, intra- and interspecific interactions, and stand age. In the short term, individuals acclimate to local conditions by adjusting their photosynthetic activity in response to temperature and water availability. As such, over time, changes in forest cover, whether through afforestation or deforestation, will affect water availability in the forest and downstream. papers.source: Asian Journal of Agriculture and Biology
papers.summary: The groundwater resources of the Ravi river basin are facing increasing pressure due to agricultural, domestic, industrial and urban water needs.However, groundwater changes in this basin have not been assessed using a spatially distributed modelling approach.This study used MODFLOW-NWT to assess spatial and temporal fluctuations in groundwater levels across 12 districts of Punjab, Pakistan.The model integrated land-use, soil, climatic and groundwater data.The aquifer was divided into three layers of 80 m, 120 m and 300 m, using a grid size of 6 km × 6 km.Data from 739 piezometric wells (2000-2019) were used for model calibration and validation.During calibration, R², Pearson r and NSE ranged from 0.77-0.84,0.77-0.84and 0.91-0.95,respectively.During validation, the corresponding values ranged from 0.89-0.92,0.98 and 0.89-0.92,respectively.The results indicate that groundwater levels declined at an average rate of 0.5-1.0m/year, reaching 2-3 m/year in some areas, particularly around Lahore, Sheikhupura, Faisalabad and Pakpattan.Sensitivity analysis using the Parameter Estimation (PEST) package evaluated the influence of horizontal (Kh) and vertical (Kv) hydraulic conductivity, recharge (RCH), specific yield (Sy) and specific storage (Ss).Groundwater depletion was spatially variable and particularly significant in areas with high agricultural and urban water demand.Although the 6 km × 6 km grid supports regional assessment, it may not capture local groundwater variations.This quantitative assessment can support regional groundwater management by identifying depletion hotspots and informing targeted interventions, including rainwater harvesting and managed aquifer recharge, to improve groundwater storage and recovery.

papers.title: Assessing machine learning algorithms for prediction of soil infiltration behavior in semi-arid agricultural soils
papers.summary: Accurate estimation of soil infiltration characteristics is fundamental for irrigation design, hydrological modeling, and sustainable soil and water management. However, the nonlinear interactions among soil physical, hydraulic, and chemical properties make reliable prediction of cumulative infiltration (It) and basic infiltration rate (Ib) challenging using conventional statistical approaches. This study evaluated the predictive performance of artificial neural networks (ANNs), random forest (RF), and multiple linear regression (MLR) for estimating It and Ib under three input scenarios of soil properties comprising (i) physical properties, (ii) physical and hydraulic properties, and (iii) physical, hydraulic, and chemical properties. The RF model also provided highly accurate predictions (NRMSE = 0.045–0.047, and R 2 = 0.96–0.97 for It, and NRMSE = 0.008–0.009, and R 2 = 0.999 for Ib). papers.summary: Peri-urban floodplains include a diverse range of potential contaminant sources and complex surface water-groundwater interactions which control the transport of emerging contaminants in underlying groundwater systems. The impact of an unlined legacy landfill located within the floodplain of the River Thames in southern United Kingdom is assessed with two downgradient multi-depth piezometer transects, and results compared with a control piezometer site previously shown to be unaffected by the landfill leachate plume. Groundwater samples collected from two monitoring rounds in 2017 and 2018 from a network of sites showed the landfill to be a heterogeneous source of contaminants. Over 580 micro-organics (MO) including pharmaceuticals, pesticides, lifestyle products, surfactants and per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) were screened in groundwater and surface water using an semi-quantitative LCMS screen. Use of sucralose (an artificial sweetener) post-dates the closure of the landfill. Sucralose found within the landfill plume, together with contaminants found within the control site, suggests a more recent source of contamination also contributes to groundwater contamination within the floodplain. As these samples do not match the fingerprint of the River Thames, it is proposed that the additional contaminant source could be infiltration from either a canal or train wastewater discharge upgradient of the landfill. Spatial variation shows contaminant attenuation down gradient of the landfill with higher concentrations found in the deeper part of the alluvial gravel aquifer system possibly due to local recharge diluting shallow groundwater. Although closed 40 years prior to this study, groundwater sampling has demonstrated that the landfill continues to be a source of persistent, mobile contaminants.

papers.title: Flood simulation and early warning in the XiHanShui River Basin using HEC-HMS
papers.summary: The Xihan River basin is located in the southern part of Gansu Province, where flood disasters occur frequently in summer and autumn, which easily pose significant risks to human life. In order to improve the accuracy of flood disaster predictions and early warnings, a flood model suitable for this region was constructed based on the HEC-HMS (Hydrologic Engineering Center's-hydrologic modeling system) model and used to determine the critical areal rainfall for flood disasters. Calibration of this model was performed using data of four flood events from May to October between 2020 and 2021, reserving data of two additional flood events for model validation. Using the calibrated HEC-HMS model, the critical areal rainfall was determined for the Pingluo and Tanjiaba hydrological stations in the basin through the model testing method. The results indicate that: (1) The stable infiltration rate of the XiHanShui River Basin was between 0.06 and 0.10 mm/h, with runoff concentration times primarily varying from 22.5 to 24.1 hours, a direct runoff storage coefficient was 0.2 hours, and a base flow index decay constant seted at 0.03 hours. (2) During the calibration and validation periods, the average peak flow relative error was 7.56%, the average runoff volume relative error was 14.76%, the average peak occurrence time difference was -0.5 hours, and the Nash efficiency coefficient was 0.769. (3) The warning areal rainfall for the Pingluo and Tanjiaba hydrological stations were 108.1mm and 128.5mm, and the guaranteed areal rainfall were 230.8mm and 184.6mm. The HEC-HMS model demonstrated high applicability and accuracy in simulating flood events in the XiHanShui River Basin, providing technical support for hydrological research and operational applications in the region.

papers.summary: Introduction Groundwater recharge is traditionally understood to be primarily controlled by precipitation and other climatic processes. However, intensive anthropogenic water management and urbanization may weaken this relationship in megacities. This study investigates hydrological decoupling at the municipal scale in Beijing, China, and quantifies the relative contributions of anthropogenic and climatic drivers to groundwater dynamics. Methods We analyzed 19 years of multisource hydroclimatic data using nonparametric trend analyses, antecedent-window correlation analyses, and hierarchical multiple regression. Future drought risks and groundwater trends were also assessed under the SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 climate scenarios for 2024–2100. Spatial analyses further indicated that dense impervious surfaces and managed vegetation may constrain natural recharge and weaken the influence of meteorological variability on groundwater dynamics. Both future climate scenarios indicated substantial drought risk, while historical evidence suggested that groundwater trajectories would remain strongly influenced by active water management. papers.summary: Abstract. papers.summary: Groundwater serves as a critical water source for domestic, industrial, and ecological security in valley-type cities across the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, China. Under the combined pressures of climate change and urbanization, the evolution of regional groundwater systems has become increasingly complex. papers.summary: Macroscopic interfaces, including joints and fissures, interstratal contacts, paleosol horizons, and weak interlayers, are widespread in loess tableland areas. These interfaces alter slope integrity and stress-transfer pathways while influencing water infiltration, local water retention, and strength degradation. They therefore provide an important perspective for understanding the development and initiation of loess landslides. Drawing on previous research into loess discontinuities, rainfall infiltration, slope deformation and failure, physical model testing, and numerical simulation, this review systematically examines the classification and spatial development of macroscopic interfaces, their hydro-mechanical effects, discontinuity propagation, and slope instability modes. Research on the Southern Jingyang Tableland is used to evaluate existing agreements and limitations. Available evidence indicates that macroscopic interfaces affect loess slope stability by dissecting slope masses, promoting preferential infiltration, and modifying local stress conditions. However, consistent multiscale characterization of interface geometry, progressive coalescence under hydro-mechanical coupling, and quantitative relationships with landslide kinematics require further investigation. Future research directions are proposed to inform geohazard identification, assessment, and mitigation in loess tableland areas.

Permeability anisotropy systematically deflects fluid flow in volcanic media
papers.summary: Permeability is fundamental in volcanic systems, governing heat and mass transfer across spatial scales and controlling pressurisation of the edifice and conduit. In nature, permeability is rarely isotropic and should be treated as a second-order tensor rather than a scalar. This contribution experimentally demonstrates directional dependence of permeability in transversely isotropic volcanic tuff, highlighting a critical phenomenon: other than when measurements are made parallel or perpendicular to fabric (the structural axis n), flow is deflected away from the driving hydraulic gradient. A closed-form analytical expression is derived for the critical gradient angle β^*, which describes the hydraulic gradient orientation relative to n at which flow deflection reaches its maximum value δ^*. The angle β^* depends only on the permeability anisotropy ratio. This effect has consequences for the interpretation of volcanic fluid pathways: anisotropy can decouple surface fluid discharge from the direction of the driving pressure gradient, produce lateral offsets between subsurface sources and surface expressions, and allow permeability anisotropy to be inferred from flow trajectories. Changes in anisotropy during deformation or compaction can further significantly redirect preferential flow pathways through time.

papers.title: Effects of the initiation timing of water-alternating-gas injection on displacement front evolution and remaining oil mobilization after waterflooding in low-permeability conglomerates
papers.summary: Low-permeability conglomerate reservoirs are highly heterogeneous, and preferential flow pathways readily develop during waterflooding, leaving some oil-bearing regions poorly swept. Water-alternating-gas (CO2-WAG) injection can further mobilize remaining oil after waterflooding, but how WAG initiation timing affects subsequent displacement remains unclear. Core-flooding experiments monitored by in situ low-field nuclear magnetic resonance (LF-NMR) compare WAG initiation at 80% and 90% water cut. A three-dimensional digital rock model reconstructed from micro-CT images is further used in three-phase volume-of-fluid (VOF) simulations to examine displacement front propagation, incremental sweep, and remaining oil connectivity for initiation at 75%, 80%, 85%, and 90% water cut. Experimentally, initiation at 80% water cut yields approximately 27 percentage points of incremental oil recovery, compared with approximately 11 percentage points at 90%, together with greater oil mobilization in the short-T2 range. The simulations show that these differences are associated with the development of preferential flow pathways during waterflooding and the remaining oil distribution at WAG initiation. In the 75% case, the established flow pathways are not sufficiently connected for continued front propagation. In the 90% case, subsequent CO2 and water slugs remain concentrated mainly in established pathways, limiting further sweep. In contrast, the 80% case combines sufficiently connected flow pathways with substantial poorly swept oil-bearing pore space, allowing subsequent slugs to advance along existing pathways and enter adjacent pores. This produces the largest incremental swept pore-volume fraction and promotes fragmentation of connected remaining oil. These findings show how the waterflood-end flow structure influences subsequent CO2-WAG displacement and remaining oil mobilization.

papers.title: Selective Subsurface Flow Regulation by an HPAM/Aluminum Citrate Weak Gel in Heterogeneous Sandstone Uranium In-Situ Leaching: Laboratory Experiments and Field Application
papers.summary: Preferential flow through high-permeability pathways is a major challenge in uranium in situ leaching (ISL) because it can induce hydraulic short-circuiting and reduce the effective sweep of the leaching solution within heterogeneous sandstone aquifers. In this study, a weak-gel system composed of partially hydrolyzed polyacrylamide (HPAM) and aluminum citrate (AlCit) was investigated for selective hydraulic regulation in heterogeneous porous media, followed by field-scale application. The HPAM/AlCit system exhibited time- and temperature-dependent gelation behavior, enabling low-viscosity injection followed by delayed in situ crosslinking. In parallel sand-pack experiments with initial permeabilities of 9.06 and 2.87 μm2, 350 and 91 mL of gelant entered the high- and low-permeability columns, respectively, demonstrating permeability-driven preferential placement. After gelation, permeability was reduced by 99.59% in the high-permeability medium but by only 31.01% in the low-permeability medium, while the corresponding residual resistance factors were 245 and 1.45. Field injection further confirmed the injectability and hydraulic-regulation capability of the system. The injectivities of two treated wells decreased by 61.4% and 83.3%, respectively, while the average hydraulic conductivity of the test zone decreased from 25.1 to 17.2 m/d, corresponding to a reduction of 31.5%. An inspection well located 3.0 m from the injection well recovered gel-containing cores predominantly within the target sandstone interval, providing direct evidence of meter-scale lateral gel propagation. Overall, the results demonstrate a cross-scale mechanism involving permeability-driven preferential migration, delayed in situ gelation, selective permeability reduction, and hydraulic-resistance redistribution. The proposed approach provides a potential strategy for controlling preferential flow in heterogeneous sandstone aquifers during uranium ISL.

papers.title: Prioritizing Fuel Treatments to Reduce Post-Fire Debris Flow Risk in Utah
papers.summary: Wildfire is a natural part of many forest ecosystems, but in the western United States, wildfires have become larger, more frequent, and more severe in recent decades. There are serious problems after severe wildfire, including erosion, flooding, and debris flows that threaten water quality, roads, and communities. Because of this, land managers need better ways to decide where fuel treatments, such as prescribed burning or thinning, can most effectively reduce wildfire damage and post-fire risks. In this dissertation, I studied how fuel treatments might reduce wildfire severity and lower the risk of post-fire debris flows in Utah. Finally, I applied those results to real watersheds in Utah to estimate how treatments could reduce post-fire debris-flow risk. The results showed that treatment effectiveness depends strongly on forest type. In some forests, especially ponderosa pine, spruce-fir, and lodgepole pine, reducing fuels had a strong effect on lowering fire severity. In other forest types, weather played a larger role, which made treatments less effective. Across most forests, treatments that reduced both canopy fuels and surface fuels produced the greatest reductions in wildfire severity. At the watershed scale, treatment costs and benefits also varied. Prescribed burning was generally the most cost-effective treatment. In several watersheds, including Electric Lake, Big Cottonwood Canyon, Panguitch Lake, and Rockport, cost-effective treatments provided the greatest reduction in post-fire risk for the money invested, making them especially important areas for management. Specifically, ‘Laixing’ tended to accumulate higher aldehyde levels than ‘Ezhi No. 8’ under identical conditions, whereas ‘Ezhi No. 8’ showed a higher proportion of esters and alcohols. Notably, debris-flow alluvial fan soils were associated with a higher relative share of aldehydes in ‘Laixing’; because aroma-precursor pools were not measured, this is stated at the level of the volatile profile. Our results suggest that, in this dataset, varietal differences were apparent and environmental conditions were associated with distinct volatile metabolome patterns; however, cultivar and environment effects could not be fully decoupled in this sampling design. papers.title: Re-Evaluation of Bermuda Triangle Hypothesis on Physical, Hydrodynamic, and Geophysical Analysis of Vortex Dynamics in the Western North Atlantic
papers.source: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ENGINEERING AND MODERN TECHNOLOGY
papers.summary: This paper presents a formal fluid dynamic and transport phenomena evaluation of the relationship between force mechanisms and vortex motion in the western North Atlantic. It is a domain conventionally designated as the Bermuda Triangle. The study rigorously evaluates whether empirical or theoretical physical evidence supports the existence of unique, localized forces or supernatural vortex phenomena capable of causing maritime and aviation disappearances. Applying foundational principles of continuum mechanics, geophysical fluid dynamics, and atmospheric dynamics, the paper had model canonical vortex structures including forced, free, and Rankine combined vortices and scale them against natural rotational flows such as mesoscale ocean eddies and tropical cyclones. Furthermore, the investigation addresses critical physical gaps frequently omitted from traditional literatures, defining mathematical formulations for surface wind stress vectors, two-phase methane hydrate ebullient density reductions, non-linear Schrödinger rogue wave interactions, microburst downburst mechanics, and agonic geomagnetic drift dynamics. Mapping these mathematical formulations directly to historical incidents confirms that open-ocean boundary conditions cannot sustain stationary, macro-scale forced vortices or downward hydrodynamic suction fields. Instead, vessel disappearances and the absence of wreckage are fully described by Rankine storm-core turbulence, non-linear wave slamming, buoyancy destabilization, and rapid debris advection along the Gulf Stream's high-velocity vector (𝑉𝑚𝑎𝑥 > 2.5 m/s). In conclusion, while multi-physics environmental force vectors create hazardous operational conditions, no anomalous physical forces exist within the region and there is no scientifically verified evidence of localized or supernatural vortex forces. Observed losses align strictly with standard statistical risk distributions in heavily navigated, high-energy transport corridors.

papers.title: Critical Initiation Mechanism and Multi-Field Response Characteristics of Coal Gangue Debris Flow Under Different Slope Angles
papers.summary: Coal gangue deposits may develop debris flows under hydraulic loading, yet how slope angle affects initiation and internal responses remains unclear. Flume experiments were conducted using coal gangue from western Beijing at 12°, 16°, 20°, and 24°, with large-scale particle image velocimetry, pore-water pressure, earth pressure, and MEMS measurements. Coupled PFC–FiPy simulations at 16°, 20°, and 24° examined particle motion, stress, porosity, and seepage. Initiation was progressive and spatially asynchronous, evolving from localized rolling and sliding to widespread sustained movement. Critical initiation discharges were approximately 132.19, 42.56, 59.00, and 29.10 m3/h, respectively, showing an overall decline with increasing slope angle despite a higher threshold at 20° than at 16°. Simulated high-velocity zones initially developed near the slope toe and extended inward, with maximum local particle velocities of approximately 0.347, 0.387, and 0.412 m/s, respectively. Pore-water pressure and effective saturation were relatively high near the toe, while vertical stress and porosity varied spatially. The findings suggest that increasing slope angle generally favors initiation by increasing downslope gravitational loading and reducing normal constraints, while local seepage and particle-contact variability may affect instability propagation. These findings support debris-flow hazard assessment and monitoring at coal gangue disposal sites.

papers.title: Comment on egusphere-2026-5979
papers.summary: Abstract. Debris-flow numerical models are widely used for hazard assessment and engineering design, yet many models still treat bed evolution in a simplified or uncoupled manner. This study presents faDebrisFOAM, an open-source depth-averaged solver developed in OpenFOAM® that couples debris-flow motion, entrainment, deposition, and terrain evolution within a finite-area framework. The model represents the mixture as an equivalent fluid of variable density and incorporates mass exchanges with an erodible bed layer through entrainment and deposition laws. The Terrain Modification Algorithm (TMA), developed in this work, updates the computational grid at each time step, allowing topographic changes to feed back directly into the governing equations and simulated flow dynamics. The model is evaluated through three applications: validation against large-scale US Geological Survey (USGS) flume experiments, testing in an idealized parabolic geometry, and application to the 2015 debris-flow event in the La Mesilla catchment in northern Chile. The solver reproduces the measured evolution of flow thickness in the USGS flume experiments with good agreement. The idealized application demonstrates that terrain evolution is not a passive output but an active control on run-out, velocity, flow depth, and volume redistribution. The La Mesilla case further shows that coupled terrain modification promotes surge self-generation, self-channelization, and channel-plug formation, which are absent or weakened when the TMA is disabled. These results indicate that coupled terrain evolution can modify flow confinement, stress distribution, and preferential routing throughout the simulation. faDebrisFOAM therefore provides an open-source framework for investigating morphodynamic feedbacks in debris-flow propagation.

An ATmega328P-based Arduino Uno processes obstacleclearance measurements and selects forward motion, braking, reverse movement, and turning while maintaining the blower state. A practical verification protocol is developed for ranging, collision avoidance, duty-cycle control, collection performance, battery endurance, and floor coverage. The study integrates a system architecture, functional state transitions, engineering equations, and test-ready output visualizations. Analytical relationships and design acceptance criteria are distinguished from physical measurements, enabling reproducible prototype evaluation without attributing unmeasured values to the device.

papers.title: Risk of groundwater loss from an ecologically vital aquifer induced by bed separation: an assessment using strain‑softening numerical simulation
papers.summary: The groundwater stored in the Cretaceous strata constitutes a vital water resource for maintaining ecological stability in the Ordos Basin. This study assesses the risk of groundwater loss induced by coal mining, with particular emphasis on the influence of rock strain-softening behavior. Using the Yingpanhao Mining Area as a case study, the water-conducting fracture zone (WCFZ) was characterized using underground borehole measurements. A three-dimensional distinct-element model was developed to simulate the response of overlying strata to mining, employing both the conventional Mohr–Coulomb (MC) model and a strain-softening (SS) constitutive model. The simulation results indicate that the SS model more accurately captures progressive failure and the connectivity of plastic zones in key lithological units, including the medium sandstone within the Zhiluo Formation. The SS model predicted a WCFZ height of 124 m, in reasonable agreement with the measured height of 115.5 m. In contrast, the MC model predicted a WCFZ height of 57 m, corresponding to a relative error of 50.6%. The evolution of bed separations with increasing mining advance was also simulated, revealing four distinct separation zones. Based on the simulated WCFZ heights and protective-layer thickness distributions, a water-inrush coefficient map was generated, revealing pronounced north–south spatial heterogeneity in the evaluated water-inrush hazard, with localized areas of relatively high coefficient values concentrated in the southern region. These findings highlight the importance of incorporating strain-softening behavior when evaluating mining-induced overburden failure and provide a numerical basis for identifying areas potentially vulnerable to mining-related groundwater loss.

papers.title: Antecedent rainfall effects on the stability of soil‒rock mixture slopes: influence of matrix type and volumetric block proportion
papers.summary: The antecedent-rainfall effects on soil–rock mixture (SRM) slope stability remain poorly quantified. This PLAXIS 3D study tracks displacement, pore water pressure (PWP), and factor of safety (FOS) through a six-stage antecedent rainfall sequence (−72 to +72 h; peak 0.134 m/day) across 12 configurations: three USDA matrices (Loamy sand, Sandy loam, and Silty loam) at volumetric block proportions (VBP) of 0%, 15%, 25%, and 35%. The model was benchmarked against centrifuge, physical-model, and field-monitoring studies of unsaturated and block-in-matrix slopes, and its sensitivity to rainfall intensity and duration, water-table depth and matrix strength was assessed. FOS was maximized within a narrow band, at 15% VBP in every matrix. Displacement and stability dissociated: Sandy loam at 35% VBP gave among the smallest peak-rainfall displacements (0.002 m) yet a lower FOS than at 15%, so displacement alone can understate risk. Loamy sand failed (FOS < 1.0) at 0% and 35% VBP. Localized positive-PWP cells around blocks, termed water patch zones, formed preferential failure paths. After peak rainfall, FOS fell for 72 h in Sandy and Silty loam, while Loamy sand displacement and PWP kept rising. From one geometry and one event, the VBP thresholds are model-based indicators for monitoring and field verification, not design values.

papers.title: Mechanical Response and Macro–Micro Damage Mechanisms of Sandstone Under Low‐Frequency Cyclic Disturbance After Freeze–Thaw Cycling
papers.source: Fatigue & Fracture of Engineering Materials & Structures
papers.summary: ABSTRACT Freeze–thaw cycling and cyclic disturbance jointly affect rock stability in cold‐region mines, yet their influence on sandstone damage evolution remains insufficiently understood. Sandstone from the Dasuji Molybdenum Mine underwent 0, 10, 20, 30, and 40 freeze–thaw cycles, followed by uniaxial compression and cyclic disturbance tests at 5 Hz. Acoustic emission (AE), RA‐AF analysis, X‐ray diffraction, and scanning electron microscopy characterized damage evolution and cracking behavior. Freeze–thaw cycling progressively reduced both peak strength and elastic modulus. Cyclic disturbance promoted propagation and coalescence of existing defects. Recorded peak AE energy and ringing counts generally declined, while the proportion of shear‐classified AE events increased from 31.2% to 53.6%. Major mineral composition remained largely unchanged, whereas pore expansion, intergranular debonding, and fracture development indicated progressive microstructural deterioration. These results provide experimental insights into sandstone damage evolution relevant to slope stability assessment in cold‐region mines.

papers.summary: Abstract This pilot water‐trace experiment evaluates subsurface hydraulic connectivity between an ephemeral channel and a deep fractured‐carbonate aquifer (vadose zone thickness >300 m) to assess managed aquifer recharge (MAR) feasibility in semi‐arid settings. The study site comprises an ephemeral channel incised into fractured limestone, selected for its documented infiltration capacity and proximity to structural lineaments expected to enhance vertical permeability through the deep unsaturated zone. The primary objective was to constrain groundwater flowpaths and transit times under controlled low‐flow recharge conditions relevant to MAR operations. Rhodamine WT tracer was introduced via continuous reclaimed water outflow at approximately 0.95 m 3 /min (250 gpm) over 48 h. Monitoring was conducted at two downgradient municipal wells and one upgradient site using passive charcoal receptors, water grab samples, and continuous in‐situ fluorometry. While measured concentrations were below standard quantitative detection thresholds, contemporaneous anomalous fluorescence signals were observed at a municipal production well (2.7 km downgradient) by two independent methods 11‐13 d after dye introduction, yielding an apparent groundwater velocity of approximately 200‐250 m/d. No detection occurred at the further downgradient municipal well or upgradient site. The results provide preliminary evidence of rapid subsurface connectivity in this fractured‐carbonate system. The transit time and flowpath geometry have important implications for MAR design, particularly regarding residence time and water quality. This study demonstrates that controlled water‐tracer introduction coupled with redundant detection methods can constrain connectivity in semi‐arid karst‐matrix aquifers and provides a transferable methodological framework for MAR feasibility evaluation.

papers.title: Language-Model Agents Running Verified Subsurface Multiphysics Simulations: Traced Numbers and the Modeling Choices That Still Need Checks
papers.summary: Language-model agents can now set up and run numerical simulations from a sentence, but a reported number can be wrong in two ways: the simulator never produced it, or it came from a model that was set up badly. We built GeoAI-THM Studio, an agent harness for OpenGeoSys 6.5.8 in which the language model edits only a typed model tree through 21 tools, a configuration is computed only after its verification cases pass (27 cases; 21 within 1 % of their exact solutions, official benchmarks or consistency checks, all within 2.5 %), and an output guardrail rejects answers whose checked numbers cannot be traced to the run, the model inputs or the request. In 16 runs with gpt-6-luna and gpt-6.1-terra on eight requests in heat, groundwater flow, deformation and solute transport, every number the guardrail checks in every answer was traced in this way, and Claude Haiku 5.5, standing in for a small model during development, passed 20 of 21 test scenarios, from which the eight requests were drawn. Yet both OpenAI models answered how much a 300 W point heat source raises pore pressure wrongly, −0.507 and 0.635 MPa against 0.967 MPa from the exact solution, because both had coarsened the mesh at the source, and gpt-6-luna also around it. gpt-6.1-terra had itself found that halving the elements changed its value by 0.257 MPa and called the result mesh-sensitive, but still reported it, and the scoring script, which checks procedure and provenance, passed both answers. Recomputing every answer on the mesh of its starting example exposed the errors. A sweep of the element size at the source showed the pressure within 3 % of the exact value only when the elements there are no larger than one eighth of the distance heat has spread by the first output, and the released harness refuses coarser meshes. We propose, as a hypothesis for further tests, that each modeling choice left to the language model needs a physics-based check of this kind.

Multi-model validation of the hydro-mechanical and soil–water characteristic behaviour of a slag-cement-amended iron ore tailings– bentonite liner material across compaction moisture states
papers.summary: Abstract Compacted liners made from iron ore tailings (IOT) and bentonite must satisfy strength, hydraulic and shrinkage criteria concurrently, yet these properties respond in opposing directions to the compaction water content. This study evaluates how the compaction moisture state (2% dry of optimum, DOPT; optimum, OPT; 2% wet of optimum, WOPT) governs the performance of IOT–bentonite mixtures (20–40% bentonite) stabilised with 0–10% slag cement (CEM III), compacted at British Standard Heavy (BSH) energy and cured for 28 days. Unconfined compressive strength (UCS), saturated hydraulic conductivity ( K sat ) and volumetric shrinkage ( V s ) were measured for 25 mixtures, and Gaussian process regression (GPR) was used to map the combined compliance region against UCS ≥ 200 kPa, K sat ≤ 1 × 10 − 9 m/s and V s ≤ 4%. For the 30% bentonite/10% CEM III mixture, UCS decreased from 1775 to 1800 to 1542 kPa from DOPT to WOPT, K sat from 1.37 × 10 − 9 to 1.93 × 10 − 10 to 9.73 × 10 − 11 m/s, and V s from 3.8 to 3.19 to 2.19%. DOPT was therefore the only condition that violated the hydraulic criterion, despite giving the highest strength, whereas OPT and WOPT met all three criteria. Soil–water characteristic curves (SWCCs) measured by pressure plate up to 1500 kPa were fitted with the Brooks–Corey, Fredlund–Xing and van Genuchten models; all reproduced the data closely (root-mean-square error, RMSE ≤ 0.0035) and the van Genuchten model was marginally best. Water retention increased with moulding water content. 2%WOPT placement of a 31% bentonite/10% CEM III liner is recommended.

Stability Assessment of Landslides under Coupling Action of Rainfall and Earthquake
papers.summary: Abstract Separated analyses are widely used to evaluate the stability of slopes after rainfall and earthquakes. However, the combined impact of rainfall infiltration and earthquake shaking on slope stability remains insufficiently studied. Therefore, a unique closed-form analytical solution to calculate the factor of safety (FS) for homogeneous unsaturated slopes under combined seepage and seismic forces has been proposed by modifying the conventional Bishop’s method. The two-dimensional seepage pattern was considered to capture rainfall infiltration, while pseudo-dynamic forces at each failure slice accounted for earthquake shaking. Further, an analytical search method was developed to locate the critical slip surface. Additionally, a coupled hydromechanical finite-element model was used to analyze rainfall-induced seepage, deformation, and stress redistribution. The resulting slope condition was further evaluated under seismic loading to represent rainfall–earthquake effects without implying full two-way coupling between infiltration and earthquake shaking. All these newly proposed methodologies were applied to the 2014 Malin landslide in Maharashtra, India, to replicate the landslide mechanism and identify root causes to show the application of proposed analytical solutions. A comparison with field observations and literature demonstrated that both the analytical and numerical models realistically represented the Malin landslide. Further, the proposed analytical model was validated against a numerical analysis of a real earthquake-induced landslide. The models accurately reproduced the onset, failure zone, and progression of instability over time. The present study provides the application of new analytical solutions for practical landslides, additionally offering a reference for prevention and evacuation plans.

Numerical Simulation of Landslide-Generated Waves in Reservoirs Using a Coupled SPH-DCDEM Method
papers.summary: Abstract Landslide-generated waves occur when sliding masses impact the water surface, potentially posing significant hazards to nearby areas. This study utilizes the smoothed particle hydrodynamics–distributed contact discrete-element method (SPH-DCDEM) coupling module within DualSPHysics to simulate landslide-generated waves in reservoirs, where the SPH method models the fluid flow and the DCDEM method captures the dynamics of the granular landslide mass. The accuracy and effectiveness of the SPH-DCDEM method in simulating landslide-generated waves are validated using two physical model experiments of subaerial landslide-generated waves. Using a simplified representation of a reservoir bank deposit at the RuMei (RM) Hydropower Station in China, this study conducts an in-depth analysis elucidating the key parameters that control landslide-generated waves in reservoirs. It is found that landslide thickness and landslide entry velocity are the primary controlling factors for two-dimensional granular landslides. Empirical formulas for predicting the maximum wave height and maximum run-up height for the RongSong (RS) landslide deposit at the RM Hydropower Station are developed. The results highlight the potential for more concentrated energy and greater destructive power in landslide-generated waves in mountainous reservoirs compared to those in open water areas.

Landslide susceptibility over the Tibetan Plateau in a warming climate
papers.summary: Introduction The Tibetan Plateau (TP) is experiencing increasingly frequent landslides under climate warming. Projecting landslide susceptibility across the TP requires joint representation of antecedent rainfall, soil wetness and temperature under changing climate conditions. Methods Here we use 38 hydroclimatic and slope predictors to project daily susceptibility under SSP1-2.6 and SSP5-8.5 through 2100. CatBoost and XGBoost scores are averaged to provide a common basis for scenario comparisons. Results Maximum antecedent daily precipitation is the leading predictor in both models. Under SSP5-8.5, the annual fraction of grid cells classified as High or Very High increases by 4.37 percentage points per decade and reaches 51.2% in 2100. Increased susceptibility in June and September accompanies the July–August peak. For 2081–2100, the regional mean increases from 0.3103 to 0.3198 across precipitation perturbations of 0–50%, with progressively larger increments between successive levels. Discussion These results identify spatially heterogeneous hydroclimatic responses and a nonlinear regional-mean perturbation response, informing spatial and seasonal priorities for landslide monitoring.

papers.summary: Abstract Landslides are among the most destructive natural hazards, causing substantial loss of life and infrastructure, particularly in mountainous regions. Accurate identification of landslide-prone areas remains challenging due to complex and nonlinear interactions among geological, topographical, and environmental factors. This study evaluates kernel-based machine learning approaches, namely, kernel logistic regression (KLR) and support vector machine (SVM), for landslide susceptibility mapping (LSM) in Sikkim, India. A balanced data set comprising 693 landslide and 695 nonlandslide samples was constructed using 15 conditioning factors representing topographic, hydrological, environmental, geological, and seismic conditions. The grid search method was utilized to identify optimal hyperparameter configurations. Model performance was quantitatively assessed using accuracy, kappa coefficient, specificity, area under curve (AUC), landslide density, and success rate curve (SRC). The results demonstrate that the KLR with a polynomial kernel (KLR_poly) achieved the highest predictive performance, with an accuracy of 0.741 and an area under curve (AUC) of 0.829, outperforming other KLR variants, while the SVM with an rbf kernel (SVM_rbf) achieved the highest predictive performance, with an accuracy of 0.749 and an AUC of 0.764, outperforming other SVM variants. Furthermore, the landslide density analysis showed a systematic increase in landslide concentration from low to high susceptibility classes for nonlinear models, while SRC results indicated moderate to good predictive capability across all models, confirming effective spatial prioritization of landslide-prone areas. Additionally, a feature importance analysis was conducted to identify the most significant factors influencing landslide occurrence.

papers.title: Analytical Solutions for Water Infiltration in an Infinite Vegetated Slope under Heavy Rainfall and Its Shallow Stability
papers.summary: Abstract Heavy rainfall is a common natural phenomenon. Regarding the issue of water infiltration in an infinite vegetated slope (consisting of rooted and unrooted layers) under the heavy rainfall condition, the infiltration process is divided into two stages— before and after the slope surface reaches saturation—and the corresponding analytical solutions are acquired through several mathematical approaches. Then the proposed solutions are effectively verified by two comparisons. Finally, based on the factor of safety ( F s ), the effects of key factors on the slope’s shallow stability are quantitatively investigated, and some novel findings are obtained. For example, an increased heavy rainfall rate reduces the F s , but this effect exhibits a tendency of increasing and then decreasing. An increase in transpiration rate enhances the infinite vegetated slope’s whole stability, while its influence will be declined after the heavy rainfall infiltration. The increased root tensile strength improves the F s within the rooted layer, but does not affect the unrooted layer’s stability. Moreover, compared with the “exponential” root shape, the F s within the unrooted layer is slightly lower in the case of the “uniform” root shape. Overall, the findings provide useful insights into infiltration mechanisms and shallow stability of infinite vegetated slopes under heavy rainfalls.

papers.summary: Abstract Groundwater seepage is influenced by various anthropogenic factors during urban construction, among which subsurface structures and surface hardening are two key factors. This study employed numerical simulations to investigate the impacts of rainfall infiltration on groundwater seepage under the effect of urban construction. A numerical model was established to predict groundwater level (GWL) in the phreatic aquifer (Aq0), incorporating the actual distribution of impervious surfaces and subsurface structures for a representative urban area in Shanghai. The model accounted for land surface conditions through rainfall infiltration coefficients, while subsurface structures were parameterized using equivalent hydraulic conductivity ( K eq ) derived from effective medium theory. Validation results show that the model achieved a maximum error of only 1.7%, demonstrating reliable performance in predicting groundwater seepage. There is 23.23% area with GWL declining more than 0.4 m in the actual scenario with 93% impervious surface hardening comparing without surface hardening. Prediction scenarios with varying reduction rates of impervious surface compared with the actual scenario ( R a ) were conducted to investigate the impact of surface hardening on GWL. The results indicate average GWL of the study area presents exponential decay with the impervious surface ratio. Further, the variations in GWL of Aq0 were investigated by reducing hardened surfaces in different locations with the same R a . As the proportion of underground structures in the reduced impervious surface increases, the area with the same increment of GWL decreases. Prioritizing low impact development in areas with lower subsurface structure density can significantly enhance the efficiency of groundwater recharge by rainfall infiltration.

papers.summary: Abstract A reconnaissance mission was organized by the American Concrete Institute, Committee 133, to visit the Los Grillos Bridge in Colombia on September 13, 2023. The bridge is a post-tensioned cast-in-place segmental cantilever structure featuring a box girder spanning 180 m. Situated on a slow-moving landslide, the bridge failed on August 20, 2023. Analyses indicated that the concrete crushing of the bottom slab of the 180-m-long box girder triggered the failure. This case study demonstrates that similar structures can withstand large relative deformations in the transverse direction and differential settlements, yet they remain quite vulnerable to displacement in the longitudinal direction. It also highlights the susceptibility of bridge structures in unstable geological regions.
